{{smaller block|"Elegy" ''into'' Latin verse; to ''render'' a learned discourse ''into'' vernacular. ''Interpret'', like ''render'', does not necessarily mean to change to another language, but it does mean, as ''render'' need not, to change to intelligible form, generally by following the text closely: as, to ''interpret'' an inscription; to ''interpret'' an address by a foreigner. ''Translate'' is literally to turn from one language to another, which is presumably one's own, unless another is mentioned, but the word has, figuratively, the meaning of ''interpret.'' To ''construe'' is to ''translate'' or to ''interpret'', generally by following along word by word or clause by clause; hence the word is very often used of the work of a beginner: as, the painful ''construing'' of a sentence of Cæsar's "Commentaries." In its figurative use it retains much of this meaning: as, I cannot ''construe'' his language in any other way. See ''explain.''}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' 1. To be engaged in translating, or practise translation. {{smaller block|All these my modest merit bade ''translate'',
And own'd that nine such poets made a Tate. {{right|''Pope'', Prol. to Satires, l. 189.}}}} 2. In ''teleg.'', to retransmit a message automatically over another line, or over a continuation of the same line. '''translating-screw''' (trȧns-lā′ting-skrö), ''n.'' A screw used to move any part of a machine or apparatus relatively to another part or parts, either as a part of some general action of the machine or for purposes of adjustment; specifically, in breech-loading ordnance, a screw for moving in or out the wedge in the fermeture. '''translation''' (trȧns-lā′shọn), ''n.'' [< ME. ''translation'', ''translacion'', < OF. (and F.) ''translation'' = Pr. ''translatio'' = Sp. ''translacion'', ''traslacion'' = Pg. ''translação'' = It. ''translazione'', ''traslazione'', < L. ''translatio(n-)'', transference, transplanting, version, transferring, translation, < ''translatus'', pp. of ''transferre'', transfer, translate: see ''trans-''

{{RunningHeader|transitionary|6433|translation}}'''transitionary''' (trȧn-sish′ọn-ā-ri), ''a.'' [< ''transition'' + ''-ary.''] Same as ''transitional. Imp. Dict.'' '''transitive''' (trȧn′si-tiv), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< F. ''transitif'' = Pr. ''transitiu'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''transitivo'' = D. ''transitief'' = G. Sw. Dan. ''transitiv'', < LL. ''transitivus'', transitive, passing over (applied to verbs), < L. ''transire'', pass or go over: see ''transit.''] I. ''a.'' 1. Having the power of passing, or making transition; passing over into something. {{smaller block|Cold is active and ''transitive'' into bodies adjacent, as well as heat. {{right|''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 70.}}}} {{smaller block|Acts may be called ''transitive'' when the motion is communicated from the person of the agent to some foreign body: that is, to such a foreign body on which the effects of it are considered as being material, as where a man runs against you, or throws water in your face. {{right|''Bentham'', Introd. to Morals and Legislation, vii. 13.}}}} 2. Effected by, or existing as the result of, transference or extension of signification; derivative; secondary; metaphorical. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Although by far the greater part of the ''transitive'' or derivative applications of words depend on casual and unaccountable caprices of the feelings or the fancy, there are certain cases in which they open a very interesting field of philosophical speculation. {{right|''D. Stewart.''}}}} 3. In ''gram.'', taking a direct object; followed by a substantive in an accusative relation: said of a verb, or of the action expressed by a verb. {{smaller|''Transitive'' is opposed to ''intransitive;'' but the distinction, though practically valuable, is only of minor importance, since no transitive verb is in English incapable of intransitive use, and also many intransitives can be used transitively, and verbs that are transitive in one language are the opposite in another, and so on. Abbreviated ''t.'' and ''trans.''}} 4. Serving as a medium or means of transition. [Rare.] {{smaller block|An image that is understood to be an image can never be made an idol; or, if it can, it must be by having the worship of God passed through it to God; it must be by being the analogical, the improper, the ''transitive'', the relative (or what shall I call it) object of Divine worship. {{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Rule of Conscience, II. ii. 6.}}}} {{smaller|'''Transitive copula''', a copula which signifies a transitive relation.—'''Transitive function''', a function which admits a system of transitive substitutions.—'''Transitive group.''' See ''group''1.—'''Transitive relation.''' See ''relation'', 3.}} '''II.''' ''n.'' A transitive verb. '''transitively''' (trȧn′si-tiv-li), ''adv.'' In a transitive manner. '''transitiveness''' (trȧn′si-tiv-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being transitive. '''transitivity''' (trȧn-si-tiv′i̤-ti), ''n.'' The character of being transitive, as a group. '''transitorily''' (trȧn′si-tọ̄-ri-li), ''adv.'' In a transitory manner; for a little while. {{smaller block|I make account to be in London, ''transitorily'', about the end of August. {{right|''Donne'', Letters, xliii.}}}} '''transitoriness''' (trȧn′si-tọ̄-ri-nes), ''n.'' The state of being transitory; short continuance; evanescence; transientness. {{smaller block|The worldly man is at home in respect of his affections; but he is, and shall be, a meer sojourner in respect of his ''transitoriness''. {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Remains, p. 202. (''Latham.'')}}}} {{smaller block|We . . . are reminded of the ''transitoriness'' of life by the mortuary tablets under our feet. {{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 2d ser., p. 173.}}}} '''transitorious†''' (trȧn-si-tō′ri-us), ''a.'' [< L. ''transitorius'', transitory: see ''transitory''.] Transitory. {{smaller block|Saynt Eanswyde, abbesse of Folkstane in Kent, inspyred of the deuyll, dyffyned christen marryage to be barren of all vertues, to haue but ''transytoryouse'' frutes, and to be a fylthye corruptyon of virginitie. {{right|''Bp. Bale'', Eng. Votaries, i.}}}} '''transitory''' (trȧn′si-tō-ri), ''a.'' [< ME. ''transitorie'', < OF. *''transitorie'', ''transitoire'' = F. ''transitoire'' = Pr. ''transitori'' = Sp. ''transitorio'' = It. ''transitorio'', < L. ''transitorius'', having a passageway, LL. passing, transitory, < ''transire'', pass over: see ''transit''.] 1. Passing without continuing; lasting only a short time; unstable and fleeting; speedily vanishing. {{smaller block|For the Ricchesse of this World, that is ''transitorie'', is not worthe. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 294.}}}} {{smaller block|Considering the chances of a ''transitory'' life, I would not answer for thee a moment. {{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, vii. 19.}}}} 2†. Occurring or done in passing; cursory. [Rare.] {{smaller block|That adventure . . . gave him also a ''transitory'' view of that excellent Lady whom the supreme Moderator of all things had reserved for him. {{right|''H. L'Estrange'', Reign of K. Charles (ed. 1655), p. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|'''Chose transitory.''' See ''chose''2.—'''Transitory action''', in ''law'', an action which may be brought in any county, as actions for debt, detinue, or slander: distinguished from ''local actions'', which must be brought in the place where the property to be affected is, or where the transaction in question occurred, etc.—'''Transitory venue.''' See ''venue''1. =='''Syn.''' 1. ''Fleeting'', etc. (see ''transient''), temporary, evanescent, ephemeral, momentary, short-lived.}} '''transit-trade''' (trȧn′sit-trād), ''n.'' In ''com.'', the trade which arises from the passage of goods through one country or region to another. 404 '''transjordanic''' (trȧns-jôr-dan′ik), ''a.'' [< L. ''trans'', across, + ''Jordanus'', Jordan.] Situated across or beyond the Jordan. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Abalaa. The Egyptian name of a ''transjordanic'' town. {{right|''Cooper'', Archaic Dict., p. 8.}}}} '''translatable''' (trȧns-lā′ta̤-bl), ''a.'' [< ''translate'' + ''-able.''] Capable of being translated, or rendered into another language; that may be expressed in other words or terms. {{smaller block|What is really best in any book is ''translatable''—any real insight or broad human sentiment. {{right|''Emerson'', Books.}}}} '''translatableness''' (trȧns-lā′ta̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character of being translatable. ''Athenæum'', March 4, 1882, p. 278. '''translate''' (trȧns-lāt′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''translated'', ppr. ''translating''. [< ME. ''translaten'', < OF. (obs.) ''translater'' = Pr. ''translatar'' = Sp. ''trasladar'' = It. ''translatare'', < ML. ''translatare'', transfer, translate, < L. ''translatus'', pp. of ''transferre'', bring over, carry over, transfer: see ''transfer''. Cf. ''tralation''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To bear, carry, or remove from one place to another; transfer; specifically, in ''mech.'', to impart to (a particle or body) a motion in which all its parts move in the same direction. {{smaller block|By turning, ''translating'', and removing the [land] marks into other places they may destroy their enemies navies, be they never so many. {{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|The weeping Niobe, ''translated'' hither From Phrygian mountains. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia's Revels, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|After dinner you may appear again, having ''translated'' yourself out of your English cloth cloak into a light Turkey grogram. {{right|''Dekker'', Gull's Hornbook, p. 97.}}}} {{smaller block|Now let the two parts while superposed be ''translated'' to any other position, then the piece B may be slid off and back to its original position. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XV. 660.}}}} '''2.''' To transfer from one office or charge to another. {{smaller|In ''eccles. law'': (''a'') To remove from one see to another: said of a bishop.}} {{smaller block|At home, at this time, died John Peers, Archbishop of York, in whose place succeeded Matthew Hatton, ''translated'' from the See of Durham. {{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 381.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') In Scottish Presbyterian churches, to transfer from one pastoral charge to another: said of a clergyman.}} '''3.''' To remove or convey to heaven without death. {{smaller block|By faith Enoch was ''translated'' that he should not see death. {{right|Heb. xi. 5.}}}} '''4†.''' To put into an ecstasy; ravish; put out of or beside one's self. {{smaller block|He [St. Paul] was ''translated'' out of himself to behold it [Heaven]; but being returned into himself could not express it. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Religio Medici, i. 49.}}}} '''5†.''' To cause to remove from one part of the body to another: as, to ''translate'' a disease.—'''6.''' To change into another form; transform. {{smaller block|Unnethe the peple hir knew for hir fairnesse, Whan she ''translated'' was in swich richesse. {{right|''Chaucer'', Clerk's Tale, l. 329.}}}} {{smaller block|Re-enter Puck, and Bottom with an ass's head. . . . ''Quince.'' Bless thee, Bottom! bless thee! thou art ''translated.'' {{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., iii. 1. 122.}}}} {{smaller block|Poets that can men into stars ''translate'', And hurle men downe under the feete of Fate. {{right|''Brome'', Sparagus Garden, iii. 5.}}}} '''7.''' To render into another language; express the sense of (something expressed in the words of one language) in the words of another language; interpret. {{smaller block|And ȝee schulle undirstonde, that I have put this boke out of Latyn into Frensche, and ''translated'' it aȝen out of Frensche into Englyssche, that every man of my nacioun may undirstonde it. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. xi.}}}} {{smaller block|Neither of the rivals [Pope and Tickell] can be said to have ''translated'' the "Iliad," unless, indeed, the word translation be used in the sense which it bears in the "Midsummer Night's Dream." {{right|''Macaulay'', Addison.}}}} 8. To explain by using other words; express in other terms; hence, figuratively, to present in another form. {{smaller block|''Translating'' into his own clear, pure, and flowing language what he found in books well known to the world, but too bulky or too dry for boys and girls. {{right|''Macaulay'', Oliver Goldsmith.}}}} {{smaller block|There is a magnificent series of stalls, which are simply the intricate embroidery of the tombs ''translated'' into polished oak. {{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Little Tour, p. 247.}}}} 9. To make clear or evident to the mind or to the senses without speech; convey to the mind or the senses, as by experience.—10. To manufacture from old material; especially, in cheap shoemaking, to make (shoes or boots) by using parts of old ones. [Slang.] {{smaller block|Among these things are blankets, . . . ''translated'' boots, mended trowsers. {{right|''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, II. 110.}}}} 11. In ''teleg.'', to retransmit (a message). See ''translation'', 7. ={{smaller|'''Syn.''' 7 and 8. ''Render, Interpret, Translate, Construe. Render'' is the most general in its meaning, but is usually followed by ''into:'' as, to ''render'' Gray's "Elegy" ''into'' Latin verse; to ''render'' a learned discourse ''into'' vernacular. ''Interpret'', like ''render'', does not necessarily mean to change to another language, but it does mean, as ''render'' need not, to change to intelligible form, generally by following the text closely: as, to ''interpret'' an inscription; to ''interpret'' an address by a foreigner. ''Translate'' is literally to turn from one language to another, which is presumably one's own, unless another is mentioned, but the word has, figuratively, the meaning of ''interpret.'' To ''construe'' is to ''translate'' or to ''interpret'', generally by following along word by word or clause by clause; hence the word is very often used of the work of a beginner: as, the painful ''construing'' of a sentence of Cæsar's "Commentaries." In its figurative use it retains much of this meaning: as, I cannot ''construe'' his language in any other way. See ''explain.''}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' 1. To be engaged in translating, or practise translation. {{smaller block|All these my modest merit bade ''translate'',
And own'd that nine such poets made a Tate. {{right|''Pope'', Prol. to Satires, l. 189.}}}} 2. In ''teleg.'', to retransmit a message automatically over another line, or over a continuation of the same line. '''translating-screw''' (trȧns-lā′ting-skrö), ''n.'' A screw used to move any part of a machine or apparatus relatively to another part or parts, either as a part of some general action of the machine or for purposes of adjustment; specifically, in breech-loading ordnance, a screw for moving in or out the wedge in the fermeture. '''translation''' (trȧns-lā′shọn), ''n.'' [< ME. ''translation'', ''translacion'', < OF. (and F.) ''translation'' = Pr. ''translatio'' = Sp. ''translacion'', ''traslacion'' = Pg. ''translação'' = It. ''translazione'', ''traslazione'', < L. ''translatio(n-)'', transference, transplanting, version, transferring, translation, < ''translatus'', pp. of ''transferre'', transfer, translate: see ''translate'', transfer.]'' 1. The act of translating. {{smaller|(''a'') The removing or conveying of a thing from one place to another; transportation; removal.}} {{smaller block|Made and done was the ''translacion'' [to Paris] . . . Off hed and of the glorious body [of St. Louis]. {{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 6206.}}}} {{smaller block|The solemn ''translation'' of St. Elphege's body from London to Canterbury is taken especial notice of in the Saxon Chronicle under the year 1023. {{right|''Rock'', Church of our Fathers, III. i. 352, note.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') The removal of a person from one office to another, or from one sphere of duty to another; specifically, the removal of a bishop from one see to another; in Scotland, the removal of a clergyman from one pastoral charge to another.}} {{smaller block|Does it follow that a law for keeping judges independent of the crown by preventing their ''translation'' is absolutely superfluous? {{right|''Brougham.''}}}} {{smaller block|We can quite understand . . . Richard I. meditating the ''translation'' of the Archbishop of Monreale to Canterbury. {{right|''Stubbs'', Medieval and Modern Hist., p. 134.}}}} {{smaller|(''c'') The removal of a person to heaven without death.}} {{smaller block|Time, experience, self-reflections, and God's mercies make in some well-tempered minds a kind of ''translation'' before death. {{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Christ. Mor., ii. 6.}}}} {{smaller|(''d'') The act of turning into another language; interpretation.}} {{smaller block|The chiefest of his [King Athelstan's] Works for the Service of God and Good of his Subjects was the ''Translation'' of the Bible into the Saxon Tongue. {{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 10.}}}} {{smaller block|At best, the ''translation'' of poetry is but an imitation of natural flowers in cambric or wax. {{right|''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 324.}}}} 2. That which is produced by turning into another language; a version; the reproduction of a literary composition in a language foreign to that of the original. {{smaller block|The English ''Translation'' of the Bible is the best ''Translation'' in the World. {{right|''Selden'', Table-Talk, p. 20.}}}} ¶ 3†. In ''rhet.'', transference of the meaning of a word or phrase; metaphor. {{smaller block|Metaphors, far-fet, hinder to be understood; and, affected, lose their grace; or when the person fetcheth his ''translations'' from a wrong place. {{right|''B. Jonson.''}}}} 4. In ''med.'', a change in the seat of a disease; metastasis. {{smaller block|His disease was an asthma; the cause a metastasis or ''translation'' of humours from his joints to his lungs. {{right|''Harvey.''}}}} 5. The process of manufacturing from old material. [Slang.] {{smaller block|''Translation'', as I understand it (said my informant), is this—to take a worn old pair of shoes or boots, and by repairing them make them appear as if left off with hardly any wear, as if they were only soiled. {{right|''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, II. 40.}}}} 6. In ''mech.'', motion in which there is no rotation; rotation round an infinitely distant axis. {{smaller block|A change of place in which there is no rotation is called a ''translation.'' In a rotation the different parts of the body are moving in different ways, but in a ''translation'' all parts move in the same way. {{right|''W. K. Clifford'', Lectures, II. 12.}}}} 7. In ''teleg.'', the automatic retransmission of a message received on one line over another, or over a continuation of the same line. {{smaller|This is used on long lines to increase speed of working, and also at receiving-stations, and the translation is made from the line-circuit to a local circuit containing a local battery and the}}
